question: A 62-year-old man presents to the office because of painless rectal bleeding for the past 3 months. He describes intermittent streaks of bright red blood on the toilet paper after wiping and blood on but not mixed within the stool. Occasionally, he has noted a small volume of blood within the toilet bowl, and he associates this with straining. For the past 2 weeks, he has noticed an 'uncomfortable lump' in his anus when defecating, which goes away by itself immediately afterwards. He says he has no abdominal pain, weight loss, or fevers. He is a well-appearing man that is slightly obese. Digital rectal examination shows bright red blood on the examination glove following the procedure. Anoscopy shows enlarged blood vessels above the pectinate line. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Bright red blood on toilet paper after wiping" -> "Blood on but not mixed within stool" -> "Small volume of blood in toilet bowl associated with straining" -> "Uncomfortable lump in anus when defecating" -> "Enlarged blood vessels above the pectinate line on anoscopy" -> "Grade 2 internal hemorrhoids" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Bright red blood on examination glove following digital rectal examination" -> "Enlarged blood vessels above the pectinate line on anoscopy" -> "Grade 2 internal hemorrhoids" -> 90%
analysis: The most likely cause of the patient's symptoms is Grade 2 internal hemorrhoids. The presence of bright red blood on the toilet paper, blood on but not mixed within the stool, and the uncomfortable lump in the anus are all consistent with internal hemorrhoids. The enlarged blood vessels seen above the pectinate line on anoscopy further support this diagnosis.
